title: The Way of Perfection
hook: Teresa's three foundations: love, detachment, humility

segments.voice: Yesterday, the brown scapular: the Carmelite habit in miniature, worn close to the heart. Your line was a sign of belonging. What did you notice that says who you belong to? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-four.

A handful of nuns in a small, poor convent in Ávila have a request for the woman who founded it. Teach us to pray. That woman is Teresa, a Spanish Carmelite who had pushed to start a house where the sisters could live the old Rule more strictly. She agrees, and she writes them a book. But when they open it, expecting to go straight to the prayers, she makes them wait. Before a single word on how to pray, she talks about how to live. Today is that book, and the three things she put underneath everything else.
screen: `TEACH US TO PRAY.` → `TERESA WRITES A BOOK.` → `BUT FIRST, HOW TO LIVE.`

segments.voice: Teresa calls the book The Way of Perfection, and she lays down three foundations. First, love for one another. Not a warm feeling about the community in general, but the daily kind: patience with the sister who annoys you, real concern when someone is sick. She warns against two failures, too little love, and a clingy love that plays favorites. It's an echo of the Gospel of John, in the Douay-Rheims: "That you love one another, as I have loved you." Second, detachment from created things. Not hating the world. Not being owned by it: by comfort, by possessions, even by your own reputation. Third, humility. And here she does something unexpected. She says humility comes last in her list but is the most important of the three, because it holds the others together. Why build prayer on these? Because, for Teresa, prayer isn't a technique you can run while the rest of life goes on unchanged. A person who resents everyone at breakfast will bring that resentment into the chapel. So she starts lower, in the kitchen and the hallway. Only then does the book turn to prayer, and when it does, it walks slowly through the Our Father, the prayer the sisters already knew by heart. Her order of things works outside a convent too. For Teresa, the quality of an hour of prayer is shaped by the hours around it: how you spoke to people, what you clung to, whether you needed to win.
screen: `FIRST: LOVE FOR ONE ANOTHER.` · `SECOND: NOT BEING OWNED BY THINGS.` · `THIRD, AND CHIEF: HUMILITY.` · `ONLY THEN, THE OUR FATHER.` · then, large: `THAT YOU LOVE ONE ANOTHER, AS I HAVE LOVED YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one of the three. Settle, and breathe. Love: bring to mind one person you'll see today, and decide on one patient, kind thing to do for them. Detachment: name one thing you hold too tightly, and loosen your grip a little. Humility: think of one small credit you could let someone else have. Just one. If you pray, you can offer it to God. If you don't, simply hold the choice for the rest of these two minutes. The bell holds the time.

The Way of Perfection. Teresa's book for her sisters: love, detachment, humility first, then prayer. This week moved from the Jesuits to Elijah's mountain, the Rule, the scapular, and now Teresa. Today's word.
Your line: three foundations. Tonight, look back and ask which one held up today, and which one cracked. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Carmelite nuns, and others who learn prayer from Teresa, read The Way of Perfection as a guide to community life and to prayer, including its slow commentary on the Our Father.
